Photograph: Barry Williams for NY Daily News via Getty Images Technology New York City to ban student AI use in public schools until high school Teachers and parents have warned against AI use in schools over concerns of ‘cognitive surrender’ Guardian staff and agencies Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.22 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google New York City will ban students’ use of artificial intelligence in public schools through eighth grade, typically age 13 or 14. The prohibition is scheduled to be announced on Wednesday and will go into effect next week. The change is part of a sweeping overhaul of the use of technology in the US’s largest school district, which enrolls roughly 900,000 students a year. In another policy shift, classrooms will keep students off laptops or tablets through the third grade, age nine or 10. The city’s public school technology policies are closely watched by the rest of the United States. Teachers and parents have warned against the use of AI instructional software in schools over concerns about harming children’s mental health and cognitive development, in particular an abdication of reasoning to software, a phenomenon researchers have dubbed “ cognitive surrender ”, as well as environmental damage. AI use will only be allowed in high school, which begins in the ninth grade in the US school system. Even then, it will be limited to specific uses, such as learning about the technology itself. AI “companion chatbots” offering psychological support will also be banned. The rules allow teachers to use AI for tasks including preparing lessons or writing messages, but they are forbidden from asking AI to grade assignments. The city’s education department recommends limiting screen time to 45 minutes in class for middle schoolers – sixth through eighth grade – and 30 minutes for elementary school students. But the question remains of how to monitor AI use, since it often takes place outside the school environment. The new rules follow an initial framework published in March, which used a traffic light system to determine which tasks AI would be used for. In 2023, the school system forbade students’ use of ChatGPT, though the ban was reversed less than a year later. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives after newsletter promotion New York City schools ban AI chatbot that writes essays and answers prompts Read more The 2026 framework, which allowed students to use AI for research, exploration and creative projects, sparked fury among many parents and teachers who considered it too lenient. In response, the city’s schools chancellor, Kamar Samuels, said that leaders had “missed the mark” in their communications, adding his office would carefully review parents’ feedback for incorporation into future rules. The city had long planned to follow the March framework with a more comprehensive “guidebook” to take feedback into account, the education department has said. The department will set up a taskforce made up of teachers, elected officials, experts and union representatives. The taskforce is to produce a report in April, intended to serve as the basis for New York’s AI-in-schools policy. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-ursul.text: BRUSSELS — The EU and NATO will not back down from supporting Ukraine despite attacks against European countries blamed on Russia, the leaders of the two institutions said Wednesday. The rare joint statement came after Germany said Russia was behind a foiled attack on an airport used as a key logistics hub for military aid to Ukraine. “This was an attack using military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil — we will not tolerate it,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told reporters in Brussels. “If the intention was to make us think twice about supporting Ukraine, I can tell you it has only strengthened my resolve; intimidation will not work.” Advertisement Advertisement “If Russia thinks we will be divided by the threat, or if they think we will be deterred from supporting Ukraine, they are mistaken,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said . “Our unity is unshaken — our support to Ukraine is clear.” He slammed Russia's moves as “reckless,” describing a series of recent actions including “drones and missiles” intruding into NATO airspace, “malign activities” such as fires allegedly set at factories producing defense equipment for Ukraine and Russia's “hybrid attack” against the east German Leipzig-Halle airport. “The dangers Russia poses are clear,” Rutte said. On Tuesday, Berlin attributed an attempted Aug. 4 attack in Leipzig to Russia. Three drones carrying explosive material were spotted at or near the airport, including one that was found near a Ukrainian Antonov plane used to ship munitions. The remarks underscore growing tensions between Moscow and Ukraine’s Western allies as they increasingly blame Russia for sabotage and other hybrid attacks on their territory while continuing to send military aid to Kyiv. Last month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Russia would “adopt much harsher methods to destroy everything that enables the West to fuel Kyiv’s war machine.” Advertisement Advertisement Von der Leyen said the EU would send “rapid response teams” to help countries impacted by similar incidents and was “ready to impose” further sanctions against Russia. The bloc’s foreign ministers, who are meeting in Ireland on Wednesday, will discuss further measures against Moscow, she added. The leaders also signaled that the response to Russian pressure would include more support for Ukraine. Von der Leyen also confirmed EU countries were examining a new payment request of “several billion euros” by Ukraine to fund its air defenses, including buying advanced U.S.-made PAC-3 Patriot interceptors. Ukraine is complaining of a critical shortage of air defenses that's allowing Russian ballistic missiles to hit targets across the country. The request, first reported by POLITICO , will be examined by Commission experts on Sept. 7.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmqx.text: Image source, EPA Image caption, Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu condemned reported violence during school blockades By Tinshui Yeung Published 5 hours ago France's Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has warned that any escalation in the country's current wave of student protests would be "irresponsible", following the arrests of 164 people on Monday. The demonstrations, which began in Paris and have seen teenagers blockading their schools for days, stem from issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages. Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers." But a French union that defends the interests of high school students said the protests were a "legitimate response" to the conditions they face. Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said 12 members of the security forces, 12 students and three school staff were injured on Monday, while 180 schools were affected. He did not provide further details on those who had been arrested. The movement at French lycÃ©es, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Ãle-de-France region around Paris. Incidents of vandalism were reported, along with fireworks being aimed at police, and the protests have now spread to other regions in France. According to the AFP news agency, four high schools were reported to have been blockaded in the southern regions of Alpes-Maritimes and Var. Protests have also been reported in Marseille, the northern Lille area and Sedan in the north-eastern Ardennes. The Union Syndicale LycÃ©enne, which represents students, defended the protests in a post on social media. "Lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classes, stress caused by Parcoursup [the web platform used in France for students to apply to the first year of higher education]... These issues are by no means inevitable, but simply the result of 10 years of Macron's policies and the lack of resources in the national education system," it said. It called on students to blockade schools on Tuesday in defence of "their rights and against budget austerity". On the same day, unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants also called for a day of walkouts to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions. In response to the student movement, Lecornu said "the difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed", but that "violence must be condemned unequivocally, and its perpetrators must answer for their actions". The prime minister also accused the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of urging students to expand the movement. Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon, LFI's leader, blamed the Lecornu government for having "ordered the crackdown" on the protest, adding that the high school students taking part were "harmless". But NuÃ±ez said the demonstrations and blockades were "not very typical protest movements". "It is much more like urban violence, with a number of individuals who were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes, equipped with projectiles, who clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces," he said. "It wasn't about making demands; it was really violence in its purest form." Since the protests began, several incidents involving violence between students and police officers have been reported. In one incident, a police officer reportedly fired a round from a grenade launcher used for crowd control, injuring a high school student, according to France's BFMTV. Investigations have been launched into these incidents, the broadcaster added.
